Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
2.1 Data Source
The primary data source is the Address-Based Population Registration System (ADNKS), published annually by TurkStat (TÜİK). ADNKS is an administrative database that records the residential addresses of all individuals registered in Turkey, providing reliable and comprehensive population figures at the provincial level.
Source: TurkStat ADNKS, 2023
URL: data.tuik.gov.tr
RData file: deprem_goc.RData

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake

2.2 General Information About Data
The dataset covers the 11 provinces directly affected by the February 6, 2023 earthquakes: Kahramanmaraş, Hatay, Adıyaman, Malatya, Gaziantep, Şanlıurfa, Diyarbakır, Kilis, Osmaniye, Adana, and Elazığ.

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
2.3 Reason of Choice
This dataset is publicly available, regularly updated, and directly published by TurkStat, ensuring reliability. Also, the 2022 and 2023 editions capture the population status immediately before and after the earthquakes, making it ideal for measuring the demographic impact. Additionally, the provincial level of granularity is well-suited for comparative analysis across the affected region.
The February 6 earthquakes represent a critical turning point in Turkey’s demographic landscape. Studying their impact on population movement contributes to our understanding of how large-scale disasters reshape human geography.

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
2.4 Preprocessing
The raw data was downloaded from TurkStat in Excel format. The following preprocessing steps were applied:

Column selection: Only the province name, population and annual growth rate columns were retained.
Province filtering: The dataset was filtered to include only the 11 earthquake-affected provinces.
Type conversion: Population figures contained spaces as thousand separators and were converted to numeric format.
Derived variable: A population change variable (pop_change) was computed as the difference between 2023 and 2022 populations.



Code
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)

earthquake_provinces <- c("Kahramanmaraş", "Hatay", "Adıyaman",
                          "Malatya", "Gaziantep", "Şanlıurfa",
                          "Diyarbakır", "Kilis", "Osmaniye",
                          "Adana", "Elazığ")

df_raw <- read_excel("adnks_il.xls", skip = 2)

df <- df_raw |>
  rename(
    province      = 1,
    population_22 = 2,
    population_23 = 3,
    growth_rate   = 10
  ) |>
  select(province, population_22, population_23, growth_rate) |>
  filter(province %in% earthquake_provinces) |>
  mutate(
    population_22 = as.numeric(gsub(" ", "", population_22)),
    population_23 = as.numeric(gsub(" ", "", population_23)),
    growth_rate   = as.numeric(growth_rate),
    pop_change    = population_23 - population_22
  )

save(df, file = "deprem_goc.RData")

compute_stats <- function(x) {
  if (!is.numeric(x)) {
    stop("Error: It should take a numeric vector!")

    mean = mean(x),
    median = median(x),
    variance = var(x),
    iqr = IQR(x),
    min = min(x),
    max = max(x)
  )
  return(stats_list)

title: Deprem Sonrası Hasar ve Göç Akış Analizi
text:
Research Questions
On February 6, 2023, two powerful earthquakes struck south-central Turkey, devastating 11 provinces and displacing millions of people. This study addresses three interconnected questions:

Demographic shock: How much population did earthquake provinces lose, and was this loss driven by migration or direct mortality?
Migration destinations: Where did displaced people go, and what does this reveal about migration decision-making?
Recovery trajectory: Are displaced people returning? How complete is the demographic and economic recovery as of 2025?

As a supplementary question motivated by widespread public perception in Ankara, we examine: Did the earthquake trigger an unusually large migration wave into Ankara, and have those migrants since returned?


Code
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(leaflet)
library(readxl)
library(stringr)
library(stringi)
library(htmltools)

geo_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alpers/Turkey-Maps-GeoJSON/master/tr-cities.json"

tr_map <- sf::st_read(geo_url, quiet = TRUE)

normalize_city <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    stringr::str_to_upper(locale = "tr") %>%
    stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") %>%
    stringr::str_trim()
}

damage <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Il, ~heavy, ~medium, ~light,
  "Adana", 2952, 11768, 71072,
  "Adıyaman", 56256, 18715, 72729,
  "Diyarbakır", 8602, 11209, 113223,
  "Elazığ", 10156, 15220, 31151,
  "Gaziantep", 29155, 20251, 236497,
  "Kahramanmaraş", 99326, 17887, 161137,
  "Malatya", 71519, 12801, 107765,
  "Hatay", 215255, 25957, 189317,
  "Kilis", 2514, 1303, 27969,
  "Osmaniye", 16111, 4122, 69466,
  "Şanlıurfa", 6163, 6041, 199401
) %>%
  mutate(
    city_key = normalize_city(Il),
    total_damage = heavy + medium + light
  )

population <- readxl::read_excel("tr_nufus.xlsx")

pop_2022 <- population %>%
  rename(
    Yil = 1,
    Il = 2,
    Toplam = 3,
    Erkek = 4,
    Kadin = 5
  ) %>%
  filter(Yil == 2022) %>%
  mutate(city_key = normalize_city(Il)) %>%
  select(city_key, pop_2022 = Toplam)

damage <- damage %>%
  left_join(pop_2022, by = "city_key") %>%
  mutate(
    heavy_per_1000 = heavy / pop_2022 * 1000,
    total_damage_per_1000 = total_damage / pop_2022 * 1000
  )

tr_map_clean <- tr_map %>%
  mutate(city_key = normalize_city(name))

damage_map <- tr_map_clean %>%
  left_join(damage, by = "city_key")

pal <- leaflet::colorNumeric(
  palette = "YlOrRd",
  domain = damage_map$heavy_per_1000,
  na.color = "#eeeeee"
)

city_centers <- sf::st_centroid(tr_map_clean)

city_centers2 <- city_centers %>%
  filter(
    name %in% c(
      "Hatay",
      "Kahramanmaraş",
      "Malatya",
      "Adıyaman",
      "Gaziantep",
      "Adana",
      "Şanlıurfa",
      "Elazığ",
      "Diyarbakır",
      "Kilis",
      "Osmaniye"
    )
  )

earthquake_centers <- tibble::tribble(
  ~event, ~location, ~lat, ~lng, ~depth_km, ~magnitude,
  "1st earthquake", "Pazarcık, Kahramanmaraş", 37.236, 37.057, 8.6, 7.7,
  "2nd earthquake", "Elbistan, Kahramanmaraş", 38.089, 37.239, 7.0, 7.6
)

quake_icon <- leaflet::awesomeIcons(
  icon = "star",
  iconColor = "white",
  markerColor = "red",
  library = "fa"
)

leaflet::leaflet(data = damage_map) %>%
  leaflet::addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") %>%

  leaflet::addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(heavy_per_1000),
    fillOpacity = ~ifelse(is.na(heavy_per_1000), 0.15, 0.75),
    color = "white",
    weight = 1,
    popup = ~ifelse(
      is.na(heavy_per_1000),
      paste0(
        "<b>", name, "</b><br>",
        "Not included in the earthquake-affected provinces."
      ),
      paste0(
        "<b>", Il, "</b><br>",
        "Heavy / collapsed housing: ", format(heavy, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
        "Medium damaged housing: ", format(medium, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
        "Light damaged housing: ", format(light, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
        "Heavy damage per 1,000 residents: ", round(heavy_per_1000, 1), "<br>",
        "Total damage per 1,000 residents: ", round(total_damage_per_1000, 1)
      )
    )
  ) %>%

  leaflet::addLabelOnlyMarkers(
    data = city_centers2,
    label = ~name,
    labelOptions = leaflet::labelOptions(
      noHide = TRUE,
      direction = "center",
      textOnly = TRUE,
      style = list(
        "font-size" = "13px",
        "font-weight" = "bold",
        "color" = "black",
        "text-shadow" = "
          1px 1px 5px white,
         -1px -1px 5px white,
          0px 0px 6px white"
      )
    )
  ) %>%

  leaflet::addAwesomeMarkers(
    data = earthquake_centers,
    lng = ~lng,
    lat = ~lat,
    icon = quake_icon,
    label = ~paste0(location, " | Mw ", magnitude),
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<b>", event, "</b><br>",
      "Location: ", location, "<br>",
      "Magnitude: Mw ", magnitude, "<br>",
      "Focal depth: ", depth_km, " km<br>",
      "Coordinates: ", lat, " N, ", lng, " E"
    )
  ) %>%

  leaflet::addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = damage_map$heavy_per_1000,
    title = htmltools::HTML(
      "Heavy / collapsed<br>housing per 1,000 residents"
    ),
    position = "bottomright",
    opacity = 0.8

Population Dynamics (2018–2025)


Code
panel |>
  mutate(label = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, total / 1e6,
             colour = province, group = province)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2023,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "red", alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 2023.1, y = 0.2,
           label = "Feb 6, 2023",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "red") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COLORS, labels = PROVINCE_LABELS) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2018:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population (millions)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position  = "right",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 1: Population trend in 11 earthquake provinces, 2018–2025. The vertical dashed line marks the February 6, 2023 earthquake. Hatay, Malatya and Kahramanmaraş show the sharpest discontinuities.





Between 2018 and 2022, all 11 provinces followed a stable upward trend. The earthquake created an immediate structural break in 2023: Hatay lost 141,403 residents (−8.4%), Malatya lost 69,855 (−8.6%), and Kahramanmaraş lost 60,818 (−5.2%) in a single year — losses unprecedented in peacetime Turkey. By contrast, Diyarbakir, Gaziantep and S.Urfa were either unaffected or gained population, reflecting the uneven spatial distribution of damage.

Code
fit_trend <- function(years, pop) {
  m <- lm(n ~ y, data = data.frame(y = years, n = pop))
  list(predict = \(y) predict(m, newdata = data.frame(y = y)))
}

trend_tbl <- panel |>
  filter(year <= 2022) |>
  group_by(province) |>
  summarise(fn = list(fit_trend(year, total)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(proj_2025 = map_dbl(fn, \(f) f$predict(2025))) |>
  left_join(
    panel |> filter(year == 2025) |>
      select(province, actual_2025 = total), by = "province"
  ) |>
  mutate(deficit = actual_2025 - proj_2025,
         label   = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]) |>
  select(-fn)

recovery_tbl <- panel |>
  filter(year %in% c(2022, 2023, 2025)) |>
  select(province, year, total) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = total,
              names_prefix = "pop_") |>
  mutate(
    loss        = pop_2023 - pop_2022,
    recovered   = pop_2025 - pop_2023,
    rec_rate    = if_else(loss < 0,
                          recovered / abs(loss) * 100, NA_real_),
    label       = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]
  ) |>
  left_join(trend_tbl |> select(province, deficit), by = "province") |>
  arrange(rec_rate)

  filter(!is.na(rec_rate)) |>
  select(label, loss, recovered, rec_rate, deficit) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 0))) |>

    `Recovery Rate (%)` = rec_rate,

Figure 4: Each province’s contribution to Turkey’s total GDP growth (percentage points, chain-linked volume index, base year 2009). Negative values mean the province dragged down overall growth. The 2023 values are paradoxically not catastrophic for some hard-hit provinces — emergency spending, debris removal, and reconstruction counted as economic activity. The 2024 rebound is driven largely by the construction sector.





A key paradox emerges from the GDP data: Hatay’s 2023 GDP contribution was positive (+0.093 pp) despite losing 141,000 residents. This is a well-known feature of national accounting — emergency relief, debris clearance, and international aid all register as economic activity regardless of welfare implications. The 2024 surge in Hatay (+0.165 pp), Kahramanmaraş (+0.113 pp) and Adiyaman (+0.110 pp) is primarily reconstruction-driven, raising the question of whether organic economic capacity will recover once rebuilding is complete.

This selective migration pattern has long-run implications for household formation and social cohesion.

Special Focus: The Ankara Migration Question

“A common perception among Ankara residents is that the 2023 earthquake triggered an unusually large migration wave into the capital. Is this true? Did those migrants return, or do they remain?”

This question can now be answered precisely using the complete inter-provincial migration dataset (I_ller_Arası_Go_c_.xlsx), which covers all 81 × 81 province pairs from 2008 to 2025.

The Verdict
The perception is real — but the statistics tell a more nuanced story.
From earthquake provinces alone, net inflow to Ankara surged from an annual average of 7,050 (2018–2022) to 43,962 in 2023 — a fivefold increase. Ankara residents did see dramatically more earthquake-zone faces in 2023. That experience was real.
But Ankara’s total net migration in 2023 was only 23,960 — below the 2018–2022 average of 18,240 (and well below 2019’s 57,280 or 2015’s 51,047). The earthquake-province surge was almost entirely offset by a net outflow of −20,002 to non-earthquake provinces. As displaced people poured in from the south, Ankara simultaneously sent more people outward to cities like Istanbul, Izmir and Konya.
The gross flow data are even more striking: 232,700 arrivals and 208,740 departures — both decade records. Ankara in 2023 was a city of high churn, not high growth.
By 2024, earthquake-province flows normalised to net +4,720, while total net migration recovered to a record 52,029 — suggesting Ankara’s long-run pull remains strong once displacement pressure lifted.
In short: The influx was real and visible. But Ankara did not grow unusually fast in 2023. It churned — and within 12 months the earthquake-driven component had fully subsided.

Deprem Sonrası Hasar ve Göç Akış Analizi
text:
1.1 Research Questions
On February 6, 2023, two powerful earthquakes struck south-central Turkey, devastating 11 provinces and displacing millions of people. This study addresses three interconnected questions:

Demographic shock: How much population did earthquake provinces lose, and was this loss driven by migration or direct mortality?
Migration destinations: Where did displaced people go, and what does this reveal about migration decision-making?
Recovery trajectory: Are displaced people returning? How complete is the demographic and economic recovery as of 2025?

As a supplementary question motivated by widespread public perception in Ankara, we examine: Did the earthquake trigger an unusually large migration wave into Ankara, and have those migrants since returned?

text:
3.1 Population Dynamics (2018–2025)


Show code
panel |>
  mutate(label = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, total / 1e6,
             colour = province, group = province)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2023,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "red", alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 2023.1, y = 0.2,
           label = "Feb 6, 2023",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "red") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COLORS, labels = PROVINCE_LABELS) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2018:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population (millions)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position  = "right",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 1: Population trend in 11 earthquake provinces, 2018–2025. The vertical dashed line marks the February 6, 2023 earthquake. Hatay, Malatya and Kahramanmaraş show the sharpest discontinuities.





Between 2018 and 2022, all 11 provinces followed a stable upward trend. The earthquake created an immediate structural break in 2023: Hatay lost 141,403 residents (−8.4%), Malatya lost 69,855 (−8.6%), and Kahramanmaraş lost 60,818 (−5.2%) in a single year — losses unprecedented in peacetime Turkey. By contrast, Diyarbakir, Gaziantep and S.Urfa were either unaffected or gained population, reflecting the uneven spatial distribution of damage.

The 2023 red bars dwarf the 2022 baseline by a factor of 10–20 in the hardest-hit provinces. The green 2024 bars show that Malatya (+6.9‰), Kahramanmaraş (+6.3‰) and Hatay (+1.5‰) turned positive for the first time — a clear signal of early return migration, though still far below the magnitude of loss.

Figure 3: Actual population (solid lines) versus the linear trend projected from 2018–2022 (dashed lines) for Hatay, Malatya, and Kahramanmaraş. The gap between actual and projected values in 2025 represents the residual population deficit — people who left and have not yet returned.







Show code
fit_trend <- function(years, pop) {
  m <- lm(n ~ y, data = data.frame(y = years, n = pop))
  list(predict = \(y) predict(m, newdata = data.frame(y = y)))
}

trend_tbl <- panel |>
  filter(year <= 2022) |>
  group_by(province) |>
  summarise(fn = list(fit_trend(year, total)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(proj_2025 = map_dbl(fn, \(f) f$predict(2025))) |>
  left_join(
    panel |> filter(year == 2025) |>
      select(province, actual_2025 = total), by = "province"
  ) |>
  mutate(deficit = actual_2025 - proj_2025,
         label   = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]) |>
  select(-fn)

recovery_tbl <- panel |>
  filter(year %in% c(2022, 2023, 2025)) |>
  select(province, year, total) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = total,
              names_prefix = "pop_") |>
  mutate(
    loss        = pop_2023 - pop_2022,
    recovered   = pop_2025 - pop_2023,
    rec_rate    = if_else(loss < 0,
                          recovered / abs(loss) * 100, NA_real_),
    label       = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]
  ) |>
  left_join(trend_tbl |> select(province, deficit), by = "province") |>
  arrange(rec_rate)

recovery_tbl |>
  filter(!is.na(rec_rate)) |>
  select(label, loss, recovered, rec_rate, deficit) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 0))) |>

    `Recovered (by 2025)` = recovered,
    `Recovery Rate (%)` = rec_rate,
    `Trend Deficit (2025)` = deficit

  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover"),

Figure 4: Each province’s contribution to Turkey’s total GDP growth (percentage points, chain-linked volume index, base year 2009). Negative values mean the province dragged down overall growth. The 2023 values are paradoxically not catastrophic for some hard-hit provinces — emergency spending, debris removal, and reconstruction counted as economic activity. The 2024 rebound is driven largely by the construction sector.





A key paradox emerges from the GDP data: Hatay’s 2023 GDP contribution was positive (+0.093 pp) despite losing 141,000 residents. This is a well-known feature of national accounting — emergency relief, debris clearance, and international aid all register as economic activity regardless of welfare implications. The 2024 surge in Hatay (+0.165 pp), Kahramanmaraş (+0.113 pp) and Adiyaman (+0.110 pp) is primarily reconstruction-driven, raising the question of whether organic economic capacity will recover once rebuilding is complete.

3.8 Special Focus: The Ankara Migration Question

“A common perception among Ankara residents is that the 2023 earthquake triggered an unusually large migration wave into the capital. Is this true? Did those migrants return, or do they remain?”

This question can now be answered precisely using the complete inter-provincial migration dataset (I_ller_Arası_Go_c_.xlsx), which covers all 81 × 81 province pairs from 2008 to 2025.

3.8.1 The Full Picture: Total Ankara Migration


Show code
ankara |>
  filter(year >= 2018) |>
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      year <= 2022 ~ "Pre-Earthquake",
      year == 2023 ~ "Earthquake Year",
      TRUE         ~ "Recovery"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Year           = year,
    `Total In`     = total_in,
    `Total Out`    = total_out,
    `Net (Total)`  = net_total,
    `Net (EQ prov.)` = net_eq,
    `Net (Other prov.)` = net_non_eq,
    Period         = period

           bold = TRUE, background = "#fde8e8")

In 2023, despite a fivefold surge in earthquake-origin arrivals (+43,962 net), Ankara’s total net migration (23,960) was actually below its 2018–2022 average (18,240). Earthquake-province migrants were entirely offset by a net outflow to the rest of Turkey (−20,002).

In 2023, the red component spiked to +43,962 while the blue collapsed to −20,002 — two shocks that almost cancelled each other out. Ankara’s perception of being ‘flooded’ was real in terms of visible arrivals, but the net population gain was unremarkable.

3.8.5 The Verdict
The perception is real — but the statistics tell a more nuanced story.
From earthquake provinces alone, net inflow to Ankara surged from an annual average of 7,050 (2018–2022) to 43,962 in 2023 — a fivefold increase. Ankara residents did see dramatically more earthquake-zone faces in 2023. That experience was real.
But Ankara’s total net migration in 2023 was only 23,960 — below the 2018–2022 average of 18,240 (and well below 2019’s 57,280 or 2015’s 51,047). The earthquake-province surge was almost entirely offset by a net outflow of −20,002 to non-earthquake provinces. As displaced people poured in from the south, Ankara simultaneously sent more people outward to cities like Istanbul, Izmir and Konya.
The gross flow data are even more striking: 232,700 arrivals and 208,740 departures — both decade records. Ankara in 2023 was a city of high churn, not high growth.
By 2024, earthquake-province flows normalised to net +4,720, while total net migration recovered to a record 52,029 — suggesting Ankara’s long-run pull remains strong once displacement pressure lifted.
In short: The influx was real and visible. But Ankara did not grow unusually fast in 2023. It churned — and within 12 months the earthquake-driven component had fully subsided.

Hatay lost 141,000 residents (−8.4%), Malatya 70,000 (−8.6%), and Kahramanmaraş 61,000 (−5.2%) — losses with no peacetime precedent in Turkey’s modern history. Diyarbakır, Gaziantep and Şanlıurfa were barely touched, reflecting the uneven geography of destruction.

fit_trend <- function(years, pop) {
  m <- lm(n ~ y, data = data.frame(y = years, n = pop))
  list(predict = \(y) predict(m, newdata = data.frame(y = y)))
}

trend_tbl <- panel |>
  filter(year <= 2022) |>
  group_by(province) |>
  summarise(fn = list(fit_trend(year, total)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(proj_2025 = map_dbl(fn, \(f) f$predict(2025))) |>
  left_join(
    panel |> filter(year == 2025) |>
      select(province, actual_2025 = total), by = "province"

Figure 7: Stacked bars show the earthquake-province (red) and non-earthquake (blue) components of Ankara’s net migration. The black line is the total. In 2023, the red component spiked to +43,962 while the blue collapsed to −20,002 — two shocks that almost cancelled each other out. Ankara’s perception of being ‘flooded’ was real in terms of visible arrivals, but the net population gain was unremarkable.





Earthquake-province arrivals surged to +43,962 net in 2023 — five times the 2018–2022 average. But Ankara’s total net migration was only 23,960, below the pre-earthquake average of 18,240. As people poured in from the south, Ankara simultaneously sent more people outward to other cities. The net result was unremarkable. What changed was the composition, not the size.

Figure 8: Gross in-migration and out-migration into/from Ankara (all 81 provinces). In 2023, both reached decade highs: 232,700 arrived and 208,740 left. This simultaneous surge in both directions is the demographic fingerprint of a transit or displacement shock — Ankara acted as a way-station, not a permanent destination, for a large share of 2023 arrivals.





Total arrivals hit a decade high of 232,700 in 2023. But departures also hit a decade high — 208,740. Ankara in 2023 was a city of high churn, not high growth. By 2024, earthquake-province flows had collapsed back to near-baseline. The shock was real and acute; it resolved within 12 months.
